claims.text: High configurational entropy combined with kinetically limited inter-element diffusion primarily governs nanoparticle stability under the stated high-temperature service conditions.
The combination of configurational entropy and limited diffusion delays phase separation and ordering.
Modest surface enrichment of the noble-metal component retards oxidation and component segregation.
The initial nanoparticles are disordered solid solutions with homogeneous elemental mixing and minimal local ordering.
Faster heating rates promote inter-element diffusion relative to untreated or slowly heated samples.
Extended dwell times promote inter-element diffusion relative to the baseline.
An inert or controlled atmosphere can limit oxidation independently of segregation dynamics.
Size and electronic mismatch among constituent elements produce local lattice distortions.
Slight segregation forms a thin, noble-metal-enriched surface shell.
Differences in elemental surface energies cause noble-metal surface enrichment.
Noble-metal surface enrichment stabilizes chemically active sites by mitigating environmental oxidation and further elemental segregation.
Moderate service-mimicking thermal protocols will preserve a disordered, single-phase structure.
Moderate service-mimicking thermal protocols will cause minimal loss of catalytic or thermoelectric performance relative to the pretreatment baseline.
Rapid high-temperature annealing will enhance atomic diffusion and induce local ordering or phase separation.
Annealing-induced ordering or phase separation will degrade catalytic or thermoelectric performance.
The proposed stability mechanism holds when inter-element diffusion remains sufficiently suppressed over service-relevant timescales.
Very prolonged exposure or conditions that drastically enhance diffusion may cause phase separation.
